explanations.explanation: That's what the text says: Job cursed the day he was born (Job 3:1). His wife had told him to “Curse God and die!” (Job 2:9), but his words land on a day on the calendar instead. I think there's a lot of pain packed into that choice, friend. Remember it, because it matters as we keep going.

That's what his wife told him to do, not what Job does. She said, “Curse God and die!” (Job 2:9). When Job finally speaks in Job 3:1, the text says he cursed the day of his birth. Her words and his words are two different things, friend.

His friends sat with him for seven days and seven nights, and nobody said a word (Job 2:13). So when Job breaks the silence, you'd expect him to turn on somebody in the room. But the text says he cursed the day of his birth, and the friends aren't the target.

Job says, “May God above disregard it…” (Job 3:4). He wants that day treated like it was never worth a look. Then he adds that no light should shine on it. That's a man who wants the whole day skipped over.
Job wants the opposite. He says, “May God above disregard it…” (Job 3:4). A day that is remembered gets celebrated, and Job wants this one overlooked. Being born is the thing he's grieving here.

A blessing is the last thing Job is asking for. This whole speech is a curse, and the text says so in Job 3:1. He asks God above to disregard the day, and he asks that no light shine on it (Job 3:4). Not a single kind word for that day, friend.
Job says it right out: “If only that day had turned to darkness!” (Job 3:4). He keeps going and asks that no light shine upon it. When Job wishes something away, he does it with the lights off.
The text says the opposite. Job says, “If only that day had turned to darkness!” (Job 3:4). He's not hoping for a bright birthday memory. He wants no light shining on that day at all.

explanations.answer: That he had never been born
explanations.explanation: Job asks that the night “not appear among the days of the year” and that it never be entered in any of the months (Job 3:6). A night that's erased means nobody gets conceived on it. I think that's what's underneath all this: Job wishes his life had never started. It's a heavy thing to hear, friend.

explanations.answer: That he could start the year over
explanations.explanation: A do-over would still leave the night on the calendar. Job asks for the night to be taken away and never entered in any of the months (Job 3:6). He isn't asking for a fresh January, friend. He wants that night gone, and I think that means he wants his life to have never begun.

explanations.answer: That his friends would leave him alone
explanations.explanation: His friends aren't mentioned anywhere in these verses. They've been sitting quietly with him (Job 2:13), and Job's words in Job 3:3-6 are all about a day and a night. He wants that night taken away and left out of the months of the year. So he's talking about his own beginning, friend, not the company he has.

Job asks for the opposite. He says, “Behold, may that night be barren; may no joyful voice come into it.” (Job 3:7). He wants it silent, with no happy sounds at all. Go back and look at that verse again, friend.
That's what the text says. Job asks, “Behold, may that night be barren; may no joyful voice come into it.” (Job 3:7). Nobody is cheering on the night he's cursing, and he wants no happy voices in it.

Job says, “may it wait in vain for daylight; may it not see the breaking of dawn.” (Job 3:9). He wants that night to stay stuck in the dark with the sun never showing up. Picture waiting on a delivery that never comes, except it's a whole sunrise.
Rain doesn't show up in this verse. Job says the night should “wait in vain for daylight” and not “see the breaking of dawn.” (Job 3:9). What he's missing in this picture is light, not weather.

Job isn't talking about seasons here. The verse says the night should “wait in vain for daylight; may it not see the breaking of dawn.” (Job 3:9). It's about one night that never gets its morning. Spring isn't part of this picture.

explanations.answer: It let him be born to see sorrow
explanations.explanation: Job gives his reason in Job 3:10: “For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes.” He's saying that night let him come into the world and see sorrow. Notice he says the sorrow itself, friend. He doesn't blame the night for anything else.

explanations.answer: It brought bad luck on his family
explanations.explanation: Job never says anything about luck or about his family in this verse. His reason is in Job 3:10: “For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes.” It's about the sorrow he is seeing with his own eyes. So the text keeps the focus on him.

explanations.answer: It came during a time of famine
explanations.explanation: No famine is mentioned in this passage. Job's reason is in Job 3:10: “For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes.” The night let him be born, and now he sees sorrow. That's the whole reason the text gives.

Job says, “For now I would be lying down in peace; I would be asleep and at rest” (Job 3:13). Peace and rest are what he's longing for. After all those sleepless seven days, I bet rest sounds like the most beautiful word on earth.

Honor and fame aren't what Job asks for. He says, “For now I would be lying down in peace; I would be asleep and at rest” (Job 3:13). He's worn out, friend, and he wants quiet. Nobody's clapping in this picture.

Job does mention princes with gold in a later verse (Job 3:15), but those are the people he'd be lying near. What he says he'd have is in Job 3:13: “…I would be asleep and at rest.” He's looking for peace. A bank account doesn't come up.

Job pictures himself resting “with kings and counselors of the earth” (Job 3:14). These are the people with big titles and big plans. He sees himself lying beside them, with nothing left to do. I think that's a quiet kind of equal.

Prophets and priests aren't named in this verse. Job says he'd be resting “with kings and counselors of the earth” (Job 3:14). Those are the ones he puts beside himself. The text keeps it to people who built things and gave advice.
The text doesn't name shepherds or farmers here. Job says he'd lie “with kings and counselors of the earth” (Job 3:14). Those are the people he pictures resting beside him.

The text says the opposite. Job says those kings and counselors “built for themselves cities now in ruins” (Job 3:14). Ruins don't stand strong, friend. Even my best batch ends up as crumbs eventually.

That's what the text says. Job describes kings and counselors “who built for themselves cities now in ruins” (Job 3:14). They built big, and now the cities are ruins. Job's point is that even these great builders are at rest.

Job says, “There the wicked cease from raging, and there the weary find rest.” (Job 3:17). Both halves are in the same verse. The wicked stop raging, and the weary finally get to rest. I think Job is leaning hard on that second part.

The text says it plainly. Job says, “There the wicked cease from raging, and there the weary find rest.” (Job 3:17). The wicked stop raging in that place, and the weary find rest there too. Job is describing a quiet place.
Job says the opposite. He says of the captives, “they do not hear the voice of the oppressor” (Job 3:18). In that quiet place, nobody is barking orders at them. That's the part Job finds comforting.

Job says, “The captives enjoy their ease; they do not hear the voice of the oppressor.” (Job 3:18). The captives are at ease, and the voice that used to boss them around has gone quiet. It's like a boss's phone call that never comes, friend.

Job says, “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.” (Job 3:19). Small and great are in the same place, and the slave is free of his master. That's the whole picture, friend, and it's a picture of fairness.
Nobody is being sold in this verse. Job says, “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.” (Job 3:19). The word is freed, and the master has no hold on him anymore.

Punishment isn't in this verse at all. Job says, “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.” (Job 3:19). The slave is released from his master. That is the opposite of being punished.

Job says these people “rejoice and greatly exult when they reach the grave” (Job 3:22). They had been searching for death like hidden treasure, and when they reach it, they're glad. This part is heavy, friend. I think it shows how deep their misery went.
Dread isn't what Job describes. He says they “rejoice and greatly exult when they reach the grave” (Job 3:22). They were longing for it, so when they get there, joy is what the text says.

The verse doesn't mention regret. Job says these people “rejoice and greatly exult when they reach the grave” (Job 3:22). They search for death like hidden treasure, and they're glad when they find it. It's a heavy picture of how weary they were.

Job says, “I sigh when food is put before me” (Job 3:24). A plate of food is usually good news, and Job sighs at it. I think that tells you how heavy his days have gotten. Even the ordinary things have lost their sparkle.
No feasting here, friend. Job says, “I sigh when food is put before me” (Job 3:24). The food is sitting right there, and what comes out of him is a sigh.
The verse doesn't say Job prays at his meals. It says, “I sigh when food is put before me” (Job 3:24). The word is sigh. That's what the text gives us.

Job says the opposite. He says, “For the thing I feared has overtaken me, and what I dreaded has befallen me.” (Job 3:25). What he dreaded didn't stay away, it caught up with him. That's a hard thing to say out loud.

That's what the text says. Job says, “For the thing I feared has overtaken me, and what I dreaded has befallen me.” (Job 3:25). The trouble he was afraid of has arrived. It's not hiding anywhere, friend.
